Package com.github.jpmsilva.jsystemd.spring

Class JettyStatusProvider

java.lang.Object
com.github.jpmsilva.jsystemd.DelayableHealthProvider
com.github.jpmsilva.jsystemd.spring.JettyStatusProvider
All Implemented Interfaces:
HealthProvider, StatusProvider, EventListener, ApplicationListener<WebServerInitializedEvent>
public class JettyStatusProvider extends DelayableHealthProvider implements StatusProvider, ApplicationListener<WebServerInitializedEvent>
Provides information regarding the embedded Jetty servers of the application: as a StatusProvider, their connections and threads, and as a HealthProvider, for the systemd watchdog, reporting the application as unhealthy while all the threads of a server are taken and requests wait for one, if enabled.

For each server, named after the port it listens on, it reports the open connections, out of the maximum the server accepts when limited, and, when the requests are handled by a thread pool rather than by virtual threads, the threads running requests out of the threads in the pool, such as jetty-8080: 12/1000 connections, 3/10 threads. The threads Jetty keeps for itself, to accept connections and wait for their data, are left out of the threads running requests. A server that is not started is left out.

The servers are found as they start, from their WebServerInitializedEvent: the server of the application, as well as the server of the management endpoints when they use a port of their own. Nothing is reported until then.

The health is enabled on its own, as it lets systemd restart the application: while disabled, the application is always healthy. When enabled, it is unhealthy while any server is saturated: its pool has all the threads it can have, the most it grows to rather than those it has so far, none of them is idle, and requests are waiting for one, naming the saturated servers in the health details, under saturatedServers. A server that stays saturated usually means that its requests hang, on something that never answers, which only a restart recovers from. As a burst of requests can also saturate a server for a while, the unhealthy state should be delayed, with DelayableHealthProvider.setUnhealthyDelay(java.time.Duration): a server must then stay saturated, every time the health is evaluated, for that long.

The threads running requests, as shown in the status, do not tell if a server is saturated: Jetty may keep one of its threads in reserve, to wait for the data of the connections, rather than run a request with it, so that requests can be waiting while the status shows a thread to spare.

A server whose requests are handled by virtual threads has no thread pool to exhaust, and is never saturated.

Joao Silva
